moves.currentDescription: A total composed only of dependent things remains dependent and therefore requires a non-dependent basis beyond its members.
moves.lockedProposition: Dependent things collectively require a non-dependent basis; indefinitely many dependent members do not make their total independent.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: So this argument has two parts. The first part seeks to explain dependent things. So if you have a dependent sequence of turtles and there's a question about how those turtles exist and why they exist, then the idea is that you're not going to appeal to those very dependent things to explain their existence because that would be circular. So without a foundational reality, there would be no explanation or basis for the existence of dependent things in total. This premise does not depend on the the number of things. No matter how many things there are, whether one or many, the idea is that they would all collectively depend on something prior. It's like if you had a floor with brown tiles, and the floor is, you could say, brown, it doesn't matter how many brown tiles there are. I think this is also supported by experience. Um we've got lots of examples of dependent things. You add them together and they don't form something independent. Uh other things being equal expect a further explanation. And from this it follows that we can expect an explanation of the total of dependent things. And this gives us a reason to think there's a foundational reality.

moves.currentDescription: Expectations about contingent arrangements need not extend to underlying reality, and calling something necessary does not explain its existence.
moves.lockedProposition: Explanatory expectations for contingent arrangements do not automatically apply to underlying reality as a whole; calling a being necessary does not explain it.
